ELECTRIC BRIEFS. special dispatches to The Bee.
St. Paul, Minn., August 4.—The weather in all sections remains excellent, and harvesting operations have become general. In this section grain is ripening in magnificent shape: County averages for grain will be from 17 to 22 bushels to the acre.

WASHINGTON, August 4.—Reports from the southern states say that the general condition of the cotton crop is good throughout the south. The yield is estimated to exceed that of any other since the war.

EVANSVILLE, Ind.,—A fire broke out about midnight in the rear of Thomas Engle & Co.'s, ice house on fifth avenue, destroying the ice house sa'oon and restaurant on the corner, and three frame dwellings inhabited by Mr. Ballet, whose loss is $1500 insured in St. Paul Insurance Co. No insurance on the ice house.

HUNTSVILLE, Ala., August 4.—Full returns show a complete democratic victory. In 1878, Lowe, greenbacker for congress, carried this county by 1,300 majority. The result yesterday shows that he will be defeated in November.

NEW YORK, August 4.—Mr. Henry Beigh, president of the society for prevention of cruelty to animals, threatens to stop the bull fight announced for this afternoon, if the scenes enacted last Saturday recur.

SARATOGA, N. Y., August 4.—A heavy rain storm prevails here to-day. There will be no races, and the entries have been declared off.

DETROIR, August 4—Four scientifically inclined scamps who were in jail at Adrian for horse thieving, adultery, poisoning, etc., made charcoal in their prison and with the coal made an intense fire about a window, heating the stones so that they broke and thus made way for liberty.

WASHINGTON, August 4. — The Secretary of the Treasury has directed the Assistant Treasurer, at New York, to purchase two and a half millions of bonds on account of the sinking fund. Secretary Sherman left for New York this morning.

GLASGOW, August 5. — The wage question of the miners of this district who are now lying idle, will likely be speedily settled by the miners accepting the offer of a raise of 6d. daily.

LONDON, August 5. — Lord Chief Justice Cockburn is reported seriously indisposed.

BERLIN, August 5. — Professors Nordenskjold and Schliemann will meet the anthropological congress which assembles here to-day.

MADRID, August 5.—Spain will send an iron clad fleet to the Pacific in the event of war between Russia and China.

St. PETERSBURG, August 5.—Murderers of the missionary at Ismail have been arrested and confessed that they were inspired with religious zeal.

ATLANTA. Ga, Augurt 5.—Jack Mix, colored, ran away Monday with the wife of Luther West a colored barber of Jessup Georgia, West followed on the next train and came up with the flying pair at Way Cross Tuesday. The injured husband drew a pistol and fired three shots at Mix killing him on the spot.

CINCINNATI. August 5.—General Durbiii Ward was nominated for congress by the democrats of the 3rd Ohio district yesterday, and A. B Clark of Licking was nominated by the republicans of the 13th district.

COLUMRUS, Ga., August 5.—Tuesday night a political quarrel arose between S. M. Ingersoll a prominent citizen, and a youth named George Howard. Trouble sprang from a political discussion, Howard being a straight-out democrat and Ingersoll an independent. Finally the former drew a revolver, firing five shots at Ingersoll, two of which had a fatal effect.

NEW YORK, August 5, Balbo, the wife murderer, condemned to hang to morrow, was visited by an undertaker yesterday and gave directions for his funeral and burial. He exhibited a "devil-may care" indifference to the subject and suggested to the undertaker that his (Balbo's) measure should be taken for a coffin. The undertaker replied, that he had no tape measure with him, where upon the condemned man drew from his pocket a string and proceeded calmly to measure himself.

INDIANAPOLIS, August 5.—General B. J. Chambers greenback candidate for vice president has written to the editor of the Sun that he will continue on the ticket till the end of the campaign.

LOISVILLE, Kv., August 5.—John Langan ordered Bill Holmes, colored, to go away from his grocery store when the latter pulled a revolver and fired at Langan who then whipped out his own revolver and shot the negro dead.

MELBOURNE, August 5.—A new ministry has been formed.

WASHINGTON, August 5—Gen. Weaver the greenback candidate for president has issued a begging letter addressed to workingmen and greenbackers asking for contributions of $1 and upwards for carrying on the campaign, the outlook of which, he says is good.

DESPERATE SHOOTING AFFRAY.

New York, Aug. 2.—Franz Julius Munzburg, a Polish plasterer, and Xavier Lindouer, house painter, occupied rooms in the rear of No. 45 Forsyth street. The men quarreled Thursday, but were separated before either was injured. Late this afternoon Munzburg entered Lindouer's apartments and fired a shot which disabled the latter's right arm. Mrs. Lindouer seized a flat-iron, but Munzburg brushed her aside and pursued Lindouer into an adjoining bedroom, and fired a second shot into his face. Helpless, bleeding, and wild with terror, Lindouer fled to the street, pursued by his enemy. The third shot from Munzburg's pistol went wide of its mark, but Lindouer fell on the sidewalk. As he was attempting to rise again, Munzburg rushed upon him and fired a fourth shot into his right side, which killed him instantly. He was attempting to fire again, when seized and disarmed by citizens. Police officers took the murderer into custody. Lindouer was a German, 50 years old. His murderer stated to-night to the police he intended to kill him because he feared personal injury. It was said threats of lynching had been made before the police obtained possession of the murderer.

St. Louis, Aug. 2.—Cleus Hardin, a drunken negro, got in a row with Jim Daniels, another negro, about 9:30, in the locality known as Clabber alley. Prince Ferdinand, also colored, attempted to pacify Hardin, but being unsuccessful, turned away and started down Seventh street. A moment or two later Daniels threw a rock which struck Hardin in the face, and then ran away, whereupon Hardin attacked Ferdinand, plunging a large clasp knives into his heart, killing him instantly. Hardin was arrested.

The Ute Commission—Removal of the Indians only a Question of Time.

DENVER (Col.), August 2d.—The Tribune's Los Pinos special says: The Indians were stragging into the Commissioners' quarters all day yesterday to sign a treat. The chiefs having signed the agreement, the others are fearful that unless their names are forwarded to Washington they will receive no part of the $60,000 which the Commission is authorized to pay out as soon as arrangements for the removal of the Utes are perfected, which will probably be some time next fall. The Commissioners leave here about the 4th instant, and go to the Southern Ute Agency, except Colonel Meacham, who remains at Los Pinos to take the census. The removal of the Utes is only a question of time, and the Commission is only a hurrying matters as fast as possible. A year from this fall will probably see the reservation open to settlement, and the people of the United States and Colorado will have the pleasure of occupying the land and working for their bread as folks do elsewhere.

The Alabama Election.

MOBILE, August 2d.—The election for State and county officers took place to-day. In opposition to the regular Democratic ticket was one made up by a fusion of Republicans, Greenbackers and Independents. Verbal reports from the election officers at the closing of the polls show a clear majority for the straight Democratic ticket. Reports at the Democratic Executive Committee's rooms from the interior of the State leave no doubt of Alabama polling a heavy Democratic vote.

Mobile, August 2d.—Further returns in Mobile county show a clear sweep for the Democrats against the Republicans and Greenbackers. The lowest candidate will have 1,000 majority.

**Wife Shot by an Insane Husband.**

Louisville (Ky.), August 2d.—James Curran, who has at times shown evidence of insanity, shot and fatally wounded his wife Marie to-day. After having been declared sane by a Commission four years ago he left his family, and only returned this morning. He went to his home and said to his wife, "I wish you wouldn't be tormenting me so every night." She replied, "Why, Jim, I've been working all the time here at home." He then drew a pistol. She turned to fly, and he began shooting, the third ball entering her side and lung.

Circuit Judges and Commonwealth Attorneys were elected in each of the eighteen judicial districts, and Democrats are elected in at least fifteen. In the Eighth Congressional District the Democratic primary election nominated Phil. B. Thompson, Jr., for re-election for Congress.

**The Alaska Indians.**

Washington, August 2d.—The Commander of the Jamestown writes from Alaska that not over 200 Indians of both sexes and all ages remain on the Sitka ranche, all of the more enterprising being on sea otter and seal hunting trips. Those left started on a spree the 5th of July, but were soon checked by an armed boat from the Jamestown, the crew of which formed a protecting party to the Indian policemen. A little stabbing was done, but no one was seriously injured. The ringleaders have been subjected to a bread and water diet.

R. L. Edwards, a preacher, was called out of his residence at Galveston, Texas, on the night of the 5th inst., and shot dead by unknown parties.

ANOTHER MURDER. Dick Bross, a Negro, Killed by John Orr, a Sailor. The Tragedy Occurs in a Disgusting Dive in "Cheyenne." Bad Whisky and a Depraved Woman the Cause.
was shot at 9 o'clock last night by a drunken sailor named John Orr. The bullet lodged in the right breast, producing a wound which proved fatal in a short time. The affray took place in the basement of a frame rookery at No. 394 Clark street, owned by a Mr. Norton, and occupied on the first floor by Ben Weil, a saloonkeeper, and the remainder of the building is given up to negroes and low whites. The basement defies all description. Descending a rickety flight of steps from the sidewalk, one nearly falls over some rubbish at the bottom into a hallway about three feet wide and nearly seventy-five feet long. The apartments occupied by the miserables to be found there are reached by little doorways opening upon this walk, and the hall ends in the apartments of the main lessee, a big negro named Tom Jones. Adjoining his room is a hovel occupied by Ann Newman, a scraggy white, and her negro husband. Midway in the hall is a small opening in the wall of the building, and through this fresh air is supposed to be admitted. A pall of vegetable refuse, which stands in a pool of corruption in front of the premises, is repeated all throughout the tenement. A laundress adds heat to the stinks. An emaciated mother, with two children, all white for a wonder, keeps up a noisy din from morning until night. Kinky-baired wenches swearing at and threatening each other scarcely add a particle to the discord in this Pandemonium. The stench, the filth which covers everything, the subocating atmosphere, and the noise, make this den of untold iniquity almost as impenetrable to the civilized white as an African jungle.

A TRIBUNE reporter was across the street when the shooting happened, and at once upon hearing the shot ran for the basement. A half dozen negroes from the vicinity were there before him, and had found Dick Bross holding fast tightly to a white man, who, he said, had shot him. When they seized the man Bross fell to the floor and showed signs of speedy dissolution. In a few moments Ollicers Dollard and Holland, of the Armory, arrived. The former hastened off to the station with the white man, who, though deeply under the influence of liquor, was able to give his name, and to deny having done the shooting. Bross laid like one dead, and was pronounced to be so; the body was icy cold, and there was no perceptible pulse. Some noticed that he was faintly breathing, and caused his removal to the sidewalk above. There, surrounded by a rubble of low whites and blacks, the brawny, almost giant, black man laid for fully ten minutes before a wagon could be procured to remove him to the hospital. He rolled his great gray eyes and gurgled forth his fear of death in language that was only now and then intelligible.

"Who shot you, Dick?" was asked of him.

"Jack Orr, I think. He was a white man," Dick managed to reply.

HE CALLED FOR THE DOCTOR repeatedly, and, finding his strength giving out, asked for whisky. It was brought him, and just as the glass touched his lips he dashed it from him. He had suddenly remembered the pledge he had taken when he was liberated from the House of Correction recently. The bystanders cried, "Drink it." and he finally did so. A physician who was present when he was put in the wagon said he could not survive.

The police searched for a long time downstairs for the revolver, and the amount of filth they uncarthed was terrible to behold. Boxes, cans, pails, old stoves, bed-ticks, and washboilers were found filled with rubbish, rotten to the uttermost, and gradually being eaten up by slimy insects and other crawling things. The revolver was not found.

Upon the prisoner Orr, when searched at the station, were found a box of new cartridges (32 calibre), and some trifling articles. He was closely questioned, and denied doing the shooting. Some time later he told his story in full to the reporter, and, though intoxicated, he was perfectly clear-headed in everything he said.

"My name? John Orr. I'm a deck-hand on the propeller Fremont, and got into port yesterday. I live in Bridgeport,—Archer avenue,—my brother, Frank Oliver, engineer for the Archer Refinery, can give you the number. My age? About 30, I guess. I'm a widower. I used to work at the Stock-Yards, and elsewhere, and I guess Jack Orr is pretty well known in these parts. You see I and a shipmate we calls 'White Pants' left the boat for a spree yesterday. He got drunk first, and I put him to sleep down there where Bross was shot. With Bross' woman, did you say? I don't know whose woman she was. Bross was there anyway, and he made some talk. A black man was with us and when he and I came out, he said that Bross drew a razor on me, and attempted to cut three times. I didn't see the razor, nor get cut, but he said that's what Bross did. Then we had more drinks in Ike's saloon. I gave the other fellow money to buy a revolver, and I bought a box of cartridges to fix it, and we went back to see if Bross would cut us then. That's all I know."

"Did you fire the shot, Jack?"
"No; it was somebody else."
"Was it the negro?"
"Well, he was behind me at the time it was fired. He ought to know."

Immediately after capturing Orr the police started after the negro companion, of whom they had a good description. He was found in a few minutes seated on the sidewalk on Fourth avenue, south of Harrison street. Nothing was found upon him. His name, he says, is Frank Gilbert, and he is only three weeks out of Joliet Penitentiary, after serving a term of one year for burglary at Bloomington. He was at once placed face to face with Orr, and both identified each other. Gilbert then for the first time acknowledged that he knew something about the shooting, and proceeded to RATTLE OFF HIS VERSION.

WASHINGTON, July 20.—John Diggs, the negro, who brutally outraged Mrs. James Tschiffely last Saturday night, near Darnestown, Md., was captured last night at Mechanicsville, and carried to Rockville and lodged in jail. Shortly before 4 o'clock this morning about fifty men appeared at the jail and one of them demanded admission on the plea of identification. Sheriff Kelchner refused admittance to any one while the crowd remained, and they fell backward a few feet.

Another formal demand being made, a slight demur was made by the Deputy Sheriff at the door, but this was only the signal for an assault. The door was then broken in, despite the resistance of the Sheriff. While the door was being forced, quite a melee occurred with the officers, and even after the negro had been brought out into the open air Mr. Kelchner made another attempt to rescue his prisoner. He was immediately caught and held by two or three of the party. In his struggles he received a cut on his arm.

The crowd hurried Diggs off, his ankle irons clanking as he was forced down the road at a quick trot.

He was taken up the road leading to Darnestown, a man guarding him on each side. While being taken to the scene of his execution he seemed quite calm, and said he was willing to die. The indifference he showed is said to have awakened suspicion even among the party who thus took the law in their own hands. An effort was made to force him to relate the details of his assault upon Mrs. Tschiffely, but beyond acknowledging the fact that he committed the crime he would make no confession.

Arriving at a point on the road some distance from town the party met a horse. This had evidently been a preconcerted arrangement by confederates of the crowd, and showed that they were determined that nothing should fail. Opportunity was given for the villain to make his peace with his maker, although he appeared callous to this part of the proceedings. The necessary ropes were within reach, and the brute's hands and arms were pinioned. It was then found that the idea to place the negro on the horse and hang him by running the animal from under him was impracticable. The noose was placed around his neck and willing hands lifted his body from the ground. He made but little resistance, evidently knowing from the first that any such effort would be worse than foolish. The body was left hanging. Sheriff Kelchner stated this morning that Diggs made a full confession of the crime to him previous to the jail being forced.

A respectable physician while riding along the road was shot down by a colored man who apparently had no motive for the deed. Another negro was lynched in Maryland for outraging a white lady. And yet the republican organs would have us believe that the only reason why the South is Democratic is because the poor negroes are bulldozed. Occurrences in the South are magnified and exaggerated, while the very same things happen every day in the north without notice. What a beautiful Ku Klux story the Vanliew murder would have made if it had happened below the Mason & Dixon line. But who in this county ever suspected that this crime had any political significance? Men on trial and acquitted in the south before republican judges, and the Northern press howls about rebel juries which override the laws and set criminals free upon society. Men are tried and convicted of inciting to riot, of bribery in Pennsylvania, and before the jury can render a verdict or the prison doors can close upon them a republican Governor prepares a previous pardon, on a republican board of pardons sets them free. That is the difference between the republican North and the Democratic South. Republicans may commit the crime of theft, mis conduct in office, perjury, or any other high crime, they may disregard the constitution and the laws, and the more they do it the better partisans they are.

Party offices and honors are lavished upon them, and they are held up as noble examples of republican statesman. Rebel brigadiers who signify their willingness to be converted to republicanism for a consideration are received with open arms, and rewarded with offices, as were Longstreet, Mosby and other rebel leaders. But let a Wade Hampton be sent to the Senate Chamber, and the cry of "treason" "treason" comes from the throats of a thousand organ grinders. The republican platform so far as the south is concerned is just this; "Vote our ticket, help keep us in office and everything you ask for shall be granted you. But so long as you stick to the democracy, just so long you are rebels, just so long shall you be down trodden, your rights denied you, your ballot boxes guarded by our bayonets. You shall and must be a part of this union, but you shall not have one word to say about how the union shall be governed. Repent and we will give you all the spoils of office there are left after we get what we want. Stick to your present allegiance, and we will keep our heels on your necks until the majority is so great against us that we dare no longer oppress you." That day is fast approaching.

KENTUCKY LAWLESSNESS.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

FLEMINGSBURG, Ky., Aug. 4.—The report reached here this evening of the fatal shooting of Perry Jefferson, of May's Lick, by two negroes, and the subsequent catching and lynching of the negroes. Jefferson was under the influence of liquor; hence the scrape.

Excitement has been at fever heat for the past few days over a band of regulators, recently organized in the northern end of the county, giving notice to two of our most prominent citizens to leave the neighborhood in twenty days. One of the notified gentlemen, Mr. Charles Marshall, is the defeated candidate for Senator in this district; the other a very extensive sheep-raiser in the North End.

The election Monday in this district for Circuit Judge and Commonwealth Attorney was very exciting. After the polls had closed for the election at Centerville, this county, three men, names unknown, engaged in a fight in which all parties concerned received wounds from a pistol in the hands of their antagonists. One of the antagonists was lodged in jail in this city, and upon examination it was found he had been the recipient of two very ugly wounds, one in the back of the neck and the other in the right breast.

DR. WILLIAM A. HAMMOND, of New York, declares his belief that Dr. Tanner's forty days' fast was faithfully performed; that although there have been other alleged fasts of as long, or even longer duration, none of them is as well authenticated as this; that although the scientific results of the fast, owing to the imperfect methods employed, are not what they should have been, yet novertheless, enough has been shown to cause us to modify our views in regard to the effects of inanition on the human body.

Crosby; Secretary of State, William Jenney (renominated); Treasurer, Benjamin D. Pritchard; Auditor General, W. J. Latimer; Commissioner of the Land Office, James M. Neasmith.

A RESOLUTION has been introduced in the English House of Commons to remove the restrictions placed upon the importation of American beef through the regulations for the slaughter of cattle received from American ports. Arthur Arnold, Liberal, is the mover of the resolution.

At May's Lick, Ky., two negroes shot and fatally wounded Perry Jefferson. They were subsequently lynched.

Five hundred Chicago shoemakers are on a strike.

The Democratic Congressional Convention of the Tenth Missouri District nominated Hon. Charles H. Mansur for Representative.

WILLIAM F. REYNOLDS, former President of the Indianapolis and Lafayette Railroad, and until recently President of the L., N. O. and C. Railroad, died a few days since at Lafayette, Ind.

A mob of horsemen took John Bailz, who murdered his wife in May, 1879, from the jail at Athens, Ka., on the night of the 7th inst., and hung him. Bailz had been twice sentenced to death, and each time granted a new trial.

Thomas E. Snellbaker, fatally shot Policeman A. Chumley, while under arrest, at Cincinnati, O., on the 8th inst., for disorderly conduct.

Barney Cleveland, a colored man, was shot dead by an officer at Milan, Ia., on the 7th, while resisting arrest.

R. L. Edwards, a preacher, was called out of his residence at Galveston, Texas, on the night of the 5th inst., and shot dead by unknown parties.

At Oldtown, Craighead county, Ark., a few days since, John F. Klingensmith, agent of Streight & Co., of Indianapolis, Ind., was killed by Calvyn Smith—by blows from behind with a gun. Both men were engaged in getting out timber, and had a quarrel of two years standing, which originated in business rivalry.

On the evening of the 5th inst., Woodson L. Gunnels, a well-to-do farmer living 20 miles west of Americus, Ga., left home to visit a sick neighbor and returning home at ten o'clock at night, found his wife and nine of his ten small children in a horrible sleep from the effects of morphine administered in lemonade by Mrs. Gunnels. A note in a handwriting of Mrs. Gunnel was found under the morphine on the table, in which she stated that she had deliberately administered morphine to the children and herself with the intention of destroying them all and that she was not actuated by any domestic trouble. Medical aid was immediately summoned, but Mr. Gunnels soon died, and no hopes of recovery are entertained for three of the children. The others are believed to be out of danger.

At May Lick, Ky., on the 3d inst., Perry Jefferson was fatally shot by two negroes who were subsequently lynched.

An American missionary and his American servant, while on the road to relieve the famished population, were found with their throats out, near Ismidd, Turkey, recently. The murderers were arrested. They are two nomad Turks, and confessed the crime.

A row occurred in John Sullivan's saloon at Chicago, on the 3d inst., between the proprietor and a French sailor named Bourgoum. In the melce the latter was struck in the chest by a beer keg in the hands of Sullivan's wife. All the parties were arrested. Next morning Bourgoum was found dead in his cell. Mrs. Sullivan is held for murder.

Dennis Hayes, a milkman, was shot dead at San Francisco, Cal., on the 4th inst., by Michael Dolan, in a trifling altercation.

At San Francisco, Cal., on the 4th inst., James Cahill, an assayer, fired a harmless shot at Mrs. N. Sheline and then shot himself through the head.

Epististe Ferschneider, cook at the United States hotel, Saratoga, was shot dead on the night of the 3d inst., by his friend and roommate August Bremner. Another case of playfully pointing a pistol.

At Sherman, Texas, in an altercation on the 4th inst., a man named Weaver stabbed and killed a neighbor named Cox. Both farmers.

Deputy Sheriff Will F. Garrett was shot and instantly killed in a house of ill-repute at Galveston, Texas, by W. P. Allen, whom Garrett was about to arrest.

W. W. Taylor, deputy sheriff, attempted the arrest of Martin L. Minnott, a notorious desperado, at Montague, Texas, on the 3d inst. Minnott tried to shoot Taylor, but missed his aim and was killed instantly by the officer.

A negro at Savannah, Ga., saw a young colored girl with whom he had quarreled, in the custody of an officer on the 3d inst., and going up to her, placed a revolver to her temple and fired, killing her instantly.

Clinton Montague, an employ of Lasher's brewery, was found dead on the night of the 2d inst., at Crawfish Bottom, Frankfort, Ky., with a bullet through his head. No clue to the murder.

Early on the morning of the 3d inst., a burglar entered the premises of John McMahon, a saloon keeper, at Chicago. The latter was awakened by the noise and called out from the bedroom, when the fiend advanced to the bedside, placed the muzzle of the revolver to McMahon's right breast and fired. The bullet entered his body just above the nipple, and McMahon fell back dead. The murderer escaped.

Burguers and night prowlers are meeting with hot receptions now-a-days at the hands of law-loving citizens. The negro, Beed Evans, who killed a boy named Johnnie Dwyer, in Trinity county, Texas, recently, was taken from the Pennsylvania jail on the 1st inst., by a party of armed men and hanged.

Near Weston, Iowa, on the Rock Island road, about 7 o'clock on the morning of the 2d inst., a young man, named Owen McKay, from Illinois, employed on the farm of August Anderson, was assaulted by Patrick and Michael Radigan, living on an adjoining farm, and was pounded to death. Xavier Lindoner, a house painter, was brutally murdered at New York, on the 2d inst., by F. J. Munzburgh, a Polish plasterer. The men had a quarrel several days previous, but were separated before either was injured.

Boscrworth, an insane inmate of the poor house at Salina, Kan., rushed at his keeper with a hatchet, on the 1st inst., and was shot dead.

Simon Hoe the Hero.

We are informed by Col. Stanton, of the Palace Hotel, that instead of it being a fireman (as we have stated in an other place) who first took the hose to the room of the crazy man who had set it afire it was a colored man by the name of Simon Hoe. He siezed the hose, went up the ladder, broke open the window, had two shots fired at him, cooled him off with a dose of water, and went into the room alone and seized the man. The Colonel thinks it was a rare instance of bravery, and he was so well pleased about it that he presented Mr. Hoe with a ten dollar bill.—Commonwealth.

Colored Citizens in Council.

A large number colored voters of Lawrence met last night at the Republican headquarters. The more intelligent and indhpendent element predominated. Mr. Hickerson called the meeting to order. Doe Williams was elected chairman, and J. R. Johnson secretary. Hickerson moved that a committee of three from each ward be appointed upon the organization of a Garfield Club. The motion was voted down after a lively debate, in which Allen, Williams, Waller and Pembleton stated their objections.

Mr. Waller offered a resolution, and a long debate ensued, participated in by Waller, Langston, Smith, Gross, Hickerson, Pembleton, Allen Williams and others

Allen Williams was not in favor of anybody's party.

Mr. Langston was tired of seeing the colored men led around by the Republicans, who, in making their political calculations, always figured on the solid colored vote, as though they owned them.

Waller opposed the organization of a club of colored men, because in processes they would always be stuck at the tail end. (A voice: "They will always be on the tail end, anyhow.")

Another speaker was tired of seeing the colored vote treated as so much merchandise for the benefit of white Republican office-holders, who make $1,000 a month because of their influence over the colored men.

The sentiment of the meeting was strongly in favor of political independence. Of course that sentiment will be crushed out before election and the colored men will be driven to the polls and voted by their political masters. The Democrats will win the National election and the colored men will be left in the night of defeat holding the bag at the end of the political snipe drive.—Lawrence Standard,
